claim: SNX32 is a member of the SNX-BAR (Bin/Amphiphysin/Rvs) sub-family.
source: Here, we established that SNX32, an SNX-BAR (Bin/Amphiphysin/Rvs) sub-family member associates with SNX4 via its BAR domain
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract describing SNX32's classification

claim: SNX32 associates with SNX4 via its BAR domain.
source: Here, we established that SNX32, an SNX-BAR (Bin/Amphiphysin/Rvs) sub-family member associates with SNX4 via its BAR domain
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the results

claim: The residues A226, Q259, E256, R366 of SNX32 mediate the association with SNX4.
source: the residues A226, Q259, E256, R366 of SNX32, and Y258, S448 of SNX4 that lie at the interface of these two SNX proteins mediate this association
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 1

claim: The residues Y258, S448 of SNX4 mediate the association with SNX32.
source: the residues A226, Q259, E256, R366 of SNX32, and Y258, S448 of SNX4 that lie at the interface of these two SNX proteins mediate this association
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 1

claim: SNX32 interacts with the transferrin receptor (TfR) via its PX domain.
source: SNX32, via its PX domain, interacts with the transferrin receptor (TfR) and Cation-Independent Mannose-6-Phosphate Receptor (CIMPR)
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated experimentally in Figure 6

claim: SNX32 interacts with Cation-Independent Mannose-6-Phosphate Receptor (CIMPR) via its PX domain.
source: SNX32, via its PX domain, interacts with the transferrin receptor (TfR) and Cation-Independent Mannose-6-Phosphate Receptor (CIMPR)
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated experimentally in Figure 6

claim: The conserved F131 in the PX domain of SNX32 is important in stabilizing interactions with TfR and CIMPR.
source: the conserved F131 in its PX domain is important in stabilizing these interactions
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by mutagenesis experiments in Figure 6

claim: Silencing of SNX32 leads to a defect in intracellular trafficking of TfR.
source: Silencing of SNX32 leads to a defect in intracellular trafficking of TfR and CIMPR.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by trafficking assays in Figures 3 and 4

claim: Silencing of SNX32 leads to a defect in intracellular trafficking of CIMPR.
source: Silencing of SNX32 leads to a defect in intracellular trafficking of TfR and CIMPR.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by trafficking assays in Figure 3

claim: Basigin (BSG) is a potential interactor of SNX32 in SHSY5Y cells.
source: using SILAC-based differential proteomics of the wild-type and the mutant SNX32, impaired in cargo binding, we identified Basigin (BSG), an immunoglobulin superfamily member, as a potential interactor of SNX32 in SHSY5Y cells
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by SILAC proteomics in Figure 7

claim: SNX32 binds to BSG through its PX domain.
source: We then demonstrated that SNX32 binds to BSG through its PX domain
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated experimentally in Figure 7

claim: SNX32 facilitates BSG trafficking to the cell surface.
source: We then demonstrated that SNX32 binds to BSG through its PX domain and facilitates its trafficking to the cell surface.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by TIRF microscopy in Figure 9

claim: Silencing of SNX32 leads to defects in neuronal differentiation in neuroglial cell lines.
source: In neuroglial cell lines, silencing of SNX32 leads to defects in neuronal differentiation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by neurite outgrowth assays in Figures 7 and 8

claim: Abrogation in lactate transport occurs in SNX32-depleted cells.
source: Moreover, abrogation in lactate transport in the SNX32-depleted cells led us to propose that SNX32 may contribute to maintaining the neuroglial coordination via its role in BSG trafficking and the associated monocarboxylate transporter activity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by lactate quantification assays in Figure 9

claim: SNX32 may contribute to maintaining neuroglial coordination via its role in BSG trafficking and associated monocarboxylate transporter activity.
source: Moreover, abrogation in lactate transport in the SNX32-depleted cells led us to propose that SNX32 may contribute to maintaining the neuroglial coordination via its role in BSG trafficking and the associated monocarboxylate transporter activity.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on experimental observations of lactate transport defects

claim: Approximately 25% of the human genome encodes for integral membrane proteins (around 5500 proteins).
source: Approximately 25% of the human genome encodes for integral membrane proteins (around 5500 proteins).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge in the introduction

claim: Efficient intracellular transport of membrane proteins and associated proteins and lipids is essential for organelle biogenesis, maintenance, and quality control.
source: Efficient intracellular transport of these proteins and associated proteins and lipids (together termed 'cargoes') is essential for organelle biogenesis, maintenance, and quality control.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction

claim: Individual SNX-BAR proteins incapable of remodeling membrane in vitro undergo heterodimeric interactions with SNX-BAR proteins possessing intrinsic membrane remodeling capacity.
source: It is interesting to note that individual SNX-BAR proteins incapable of remodeling membrane in vitro (SNX5, SNX6, SNX7, SNX30, SNX32, etc.) are observed to undergo heterodimeric interactions with SNX-BAR proteins possessing an intrinsic membrane remodeling capacity (SNX1, SNX2, SNX4, SNX8, etc.) (van Weering et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to van Weering et al., 2012

claim: Defects in sorting nexin function are linked with Alzheimer's disease (AD).
source: Conserved throughout eukaryotes, defects in the function of these proteins are linked with various pathologies, including Alzheimer's disease (AD) (Kim et al., 2017)
evidence: This is stated with citation to Kim et al., 2017

claim: Defects in sorting nexin function are linked with Down's syndrome (DS).
source: Conserved throughout eukaryotes, defects in the function of these proteins are linked with various pathologies, including Alzheimer's disease (AD) (Kim et al., 2017), where they are associated with trafficking and processing (Simonetti et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2013; van Weering et al., 2010), Down's syndrome (DS) (Vieira et al., 2021)
evidence: This is stated with citation to Vieira et al., 2021

claim: Defects in sorting nexin function are linked with cancer.
source: Conserved throughout eukaryotes, defects in the function of these proteins are linked with various pathologies, including Alzheimer's disease (AD) (Kim et al., 2017), where they are associated with trafficking and processing (Simonetti et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2013; van Weering et al., 2010), Down's syndrome (DS) (Vieira et al., 2021), cancer (Sharma et al., 2020)

claim: SNX32 is also known as SNX6b.
source: Sorting nexin 32 (SNX32), also known as SNX6b (Simonetti et al., 2017), on account of sequence similarity to its paralogue sorting nexin-6 (van Weering et al., 2010)
evidence: This is stated with citation to Simonetti et al., 2017

claim: SNX32 is a component of the endosomal SNX-BAR sorting complex for promoting exit 1 (ESCPE-1).
source: SNX32 is a component of the recently identified endosomal SNX-BAR sorting complex for promoting exit 1 (ESCPE-1), a heterodimer of SNX1/SNX2 associated with SNX5/SNX6/SNX32.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction

claim: ESCPE-1 regulates sequence-dependent sorting of transmembrane cargo by recognizing and binding to a specific bipartite motif present within their cytosolic tail.
source: ESCPE-1 regulates the sequence-dependent sorting of transmembrane cargo by recognizing and binding to a specific bipartite motif present within their cytosolic tail, an interaction mediated by the SNX5, SNX6, and SNX32 subunits (Simonetti et al., 2019; Simonetti et al., 2017; Kvainickas et al., 2017; Wassmer et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations

claim: The ESCPE-1 complex identifies a bipartite signal sequence (Ф × Ω × Ф where Ф is hydrophobic and Ω is amino acid with aromatic side chains) present in the cytosolic tail of prototypical cargoes.
source: The previous reports suggest that the ESCPE-1 complex identifies a bipartite signal sequence (Ф × Ω × Ф where Ф is hydrophobic and Ω is amino acid with aromatic side chains) present in the cytosolic tail of the prototypical cargoes and assists in its retrieval and recycling to TGN as well as to the surface (Simonetti et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Simonetti et al., 2019

claim: SNX32 is absent in non-higher metazoans.
source: Moreover, SNX32 is absent in non-higher metazoans, and in humans, its expression is higher in the brain compared to other tissues (http://www.gtexportal.org/home/gene/SNX32).
evidence: This is stated with reference to GTEx portal data

claim: In humans, SNX32 expression is higher in the brain compared to other tissues.
source: Moreover, SNX32 is absent in non-higher metazoans, and in humans, its expression is higher in the brain compared to other tissues (http://www.gtexportal.org/home/gene/SNX32).

claim: GFP-SNX4 efficiently precipitated HA-SNX32 with a ratio of 0.92.

evidence: This is a quantitative result from co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 1A and B

claim: GFP-SNX8 precipitated HA-SNX32 with a ratio of 0.62.
